I've been farming these fields in Quzhou for over forty years, and I know what this land can do. At sixty-eight, I don't have the back for chasing after newfangled crops or wrestling with cotton that needs spraying every other week. My family has about eight mu, and the wheat-maize double cropping system has never let us down. The winter wheat is already in the ground from last October—that's how we do things here on the North China Plain. I sowed an improved variety, something like Jimai 22 or Luyuan 502, the kind that stands up to the spring winds and gives a full grain head. I'll rotary-till the fields after the maize harvest each year to prepare the seedbed for wheat, but for the summer maize, I plant straight into the wheat stubble with no-tillage. Saves time, saves diesel, and the soil holds moisture better.

This spring, I'll topdress the wheat with urea when it greens up—about forty jin of nitrogen per mu overall, split between basal and topdressing. A little phosphorus and potassium go in with the compound fertilizer at sowing, maybe six and four kilograms per mu. The wheat needs three good irrigations: the green-up water, the jointing water, and the grain-filling water. I'll spray twice for insects, once for weeds, and once for fungus when the weather turns humid. Come early June, I'll harvest the wheat and immediately plant Dengai 605 hybrid maize—that seed is what everyone around here uses because it fills out heavy and resists lodging. The maize gets about twenty kilograms of nitrogen per mu, two irrigations if the summer rains cooperate, and three rounds of chemicals total. I expect a thousand jin per mu of wheat and eleven hundred of maize. It's not fancy, but it's honest work, and at my age, honest and reliable is what I need.
